title: Area of Compound Shapes
content:
# Area of Compound Shapes

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Break compound shapes into simpler shapes (rectangles, triangles, trapeziums)
- Calculate the total area by adding or subtracting component areas
- Identify missing dimensions from given information
- Tackle real-world problems involving irregular floor plans and land areas

## Introduction

Most real-world shapes are not simple rectangles or triangles. A room might be L-shaped, a garden might have a triangular extension, or a plot of land might combine several different shapes. To find the area of these **compound shapes** (also called **composite shapes**), we split them into simpler shapes whose areas we can calculate.

## Key Concepts

A **compound shape** is a shape made up of two or more simple shapes joined together.

There are two main strategies:

1. **Addition method:** Split the compound shape into simpler shapes, find each area, then **add** them together.
2. **Subtraction method:** Start with a larger simple shape that encloses the compound shape, then **subtract** the parts that are not included.

> **Tip:** Choose whichever method gives you the simplest calculation. Sometimes subtraction is much easier.

## Worked Examples

### Example 1: L-Shaped Room (Addition Method)
**Question:** An L-shaped room has the following dimensions: overall length 10 m, overall width 7 m. The cut-out is 4 m wide and 3 m deep. Find the area.

**Solution (Addition):**
Split into two rectangles:
- Rectangle 1: $10 \times (7 - 4) = 10 \times 3 = 30$ m$^2$ (the full-width strip along the bottom)
- Rectangle 2: $(10 - 3) \times 4 = 7 \times 4 = 28$ m$^2$ (the taller strip minus the cut-out depth... actually, let us be more careful.)

Let us use clear labelling. Split horizontally:
- Bottom rectangle: $10 \times 4 = 40$ m$^2$ (full width, height = $7 - 3 = 4$ m)
- Top rectangle: $(10 - 4) \times 3 = 6 \times 3 = 18$ m$^2$

$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{total}} &= 40 + 18 \\ &= 58 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

**Alternative (Subtraction):**
- Full rectangle: $10 \times 7 = 70$ m$^2$
- Cut-out: $4 \times 3 = 12$ m$^2$

$$A = 70 - 12 = 58 \text{ m}^2$$

---

### Example 2: Rectangle with Triangle on Top
**Question:** A shape consists of a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm with an isosceles triangle on top. The triangle has the same 8 cm base and a height of 3 cm. Find the total area.

**Solution:**
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{rectangle}} &= 8 \times 5 = 40 \text{ cm}^2 \\ A_{\text{triangle}} &= \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 3 = 12 \text{ cm}^2 \\ A_{\text{total}} &= 40 + 12 = 52 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

---

### Example 3: Subtraction Method
**Question:** A rectangular piece of card measures 20 cm by 15 cm. A triangle with base 8 cm and height 6 cm is cut from one corner. Find the remaining area.

**Solution:**
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{rectangle}} &= 20 \times 15 = 300 \text{ cm}^2 \\ A_{\text{triangle}} &= \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 6 = 24 \text{ cm}^2 \\ A_{\text{remaining}} &= 300 - 24 = 276 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

---

### Example 4: T-Shaped Cross-Section
**Question:** A T-shaped cross-section consists of a horizontal rectangle 12 cm by 3 cm on top, and a vertical rectangle 4 cm by 8 cm below (centred). Find the total area.

**Solution:**
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\text{top}} &= 12 \times 3 = 36 \text{ cm}^2 \\ A_{\text{bottom}} &= 4 \times 8 = 32 \text{ cm}^2 \\ A_{\text{total}} &= 36 + 32 = 68 \text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}$$

---

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Why It's Wrong | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Counting an overlapping region twice | If shapes overlap, you add the overlap area extra | Make sure your split has no overlaps |
| Forgetting a section when splitting | Leads to an undercount | Check that all parts are included |
| Using wrong dimensions for sub-shapes | Not carefully identifying which lengths belong to which part | Label your diagram clearly |
| Using the subtraction method but forgetting to subtract | Just computing the enclosing shape's area | Remember to subtract the removed pieces |

## Summary

- A **compound shape** is made from simpler shapes combined.
- Use the **addition method**: split into parts and add the areas.
- Use the **subtraction method**: calculate a larger shape and subtract removed pieces.
- Always identify all dimensions carefully and label your diagram.
- Check that all parts are accounted for and there are no overlaps or gaps.
